view: In the neighboring trial clause the lam marks the eventual outcome: people asked whether God had favored the poor; the question about God's knowledge of gratitude confirms the point.
The prefixed kaf in 'thus We tested' intensifies the demonstrative and presents the trial as complete and remarkable.
An unrelated poetic example uses ahrazu for polytheists' seizure of Muslims' collected spoils.
The lost-sheep parable depicts a shepherd seeking a straying sheep and illustrates divine affection for those returning from error and prophetic concern for faith.
The related Ikrima report says 6:53 addressed Quraysh leaders and their clients; Umar apologized and the greeting of believers followed in 6:54.
A report has al-Sari meet Bahlul in a cemetery; Bahlul praises the dead for neither harming nor gossiping and recites verses treating hunger as pious before eventual satisfaction.
Abu Hayyan's source at this point reproduces Quran 6:36-52 without commentary.
Reports assigning neighboring verses to enemies of the Prophet's family are applications or inward interpretations rather than separate revelation occasions.
The Prophet's refusal to favor status-conscious leaders reflects religion's preference for sincere devotion over social rank.
God knows who is grateful for Islam and therefore merits guidance, answering the elites' question about favoring the poor believers.
God tested people through one another; wealthy elites scorned poor believers whose faith gave them religious precedence despite their worldly poverty.
Al-Jubbai identifies the trial as the difficult duty of nobles to believe and give precedence to earlier poor believers; the latter should accept the Prophet's honor.
Veiled people see only poverty and outward appearance and scorn the hidden rank of God-oriented believers.

A report calls deniers of divine decree and independent-human-will advocates the community's Magians; explanations dispute whether the charge applies to deniers or affirmers of decree, and a conflicting manuscript form is ascribed to corruption.
God is said to test people though He needs no information, because He treats them as a tester would.
Farahi discussed the theme in his commentary on Surah Abas; 80:1-10 likewise admonishes the Prophet over a poor blind visitor and wealthy Makkans.
The verse's lesson may remain general even if a reported incident only occasioned its recitation or application.
Sahl says pure food marks the most ascetic, strict obedience the most devout, sincerity to creatures the most beloved, and squandered time a wasted lifespan.
A servant should rely on divine mercy and care rather than other creatures or even personal deeds and states.
The superior should be grateful and the lesser patient; love can make the lesser's gratitude equal, as poems thank the beloved even for blame or harm.
The unified seekers have no intermediary account through the Prophet; absorbed in God, they do not occupy themselves with his mission, while expelling them would break their presence.
A Persian couplet contrasts noble servants of God with the speaker's wretched group.
Ṭard means banishment or expulsion, with a connotation of humiliation or dismissive disregard; ṭarīd is an expelled person.
The prohibition verb is jussive, with kasra inserted to separate adjacent vowelless consonants.
The renewed relative description rather than a pronoun grounds their right to the Prophet's company in continual, sincere invocation.
Addressing Muhammad rather than Quraysh indirectly exposes the chiefs' pride and their claim that poor believers kept them away; sincere seekers could attend without judging others.
The protected worshippers were poor, socially weak Muslims; lists name Bilal, Ammar, Suhayb, Khabbab, Salman, Ibn Masud, al-Miqdad, and various freedmen and allies.
note: Some lists add Murthid, Subayh, Dhul-Shimalayn, Mihja, Amir ibn Fuhayra, Salim, Waqid, Amr and others.

view: Mujahid identifies the callers particularly as Bilal and Ibn Umm Abd, though another transmission says Ibn Umm Ma'bad or Ibn Umm Maktum.
Quraysh or Meccan leaders demanded that the Prophet exclude poor, low-status believers from his company, promising to sit with him or follow him if he did so; the prohibition followed.
note: Names vary across reports; the shared point is the chiefs' demand and the verse's refusal.

view: Abu Talib was approached to ask Muhammad to dismiss poor followers; Umar suggested temporarily trying the leaders' demand, then apologized after the verse came.
Al-Aqra and Uyayna requested private access away from poor believers, fearing the sight of sitting with them before visitors; a written agreement was proposed or begun, but revelation stopped it.
note: Accounts differ on whether the Prophet agreed, considered the proposal, or refused it.

view: Some chiefs proposed separate days, or one gathering in which the Prophet would face them and turn his back on the poor believers.
A different account says the chiefs sought precedence in the prayer rows, moving the poor worshippers behind them rather than removing them from the Prophet's gathering.
In one account Uyayna objected to the smell of Bilal, Salman, Suhayb and other poor Muslims, offering to follow if they were expelled.
One report says a man ashamed to be seen with Salman and Bilal requested their dismissal; the Prophet was then instructed to greet the believers and promise mercy.
Some reports identify six poor companions as the occasion, including Sa'd, Ibn Masud, Suhayb, Ammar, al-Miqdad, and Bilal, while another list includes a Hudhayli and two unnamed men.
note: Al-Wahidi supplies names for four companions unnamed in one version.

view: Khabbab and Salman said the verse was revealed about themselves and the poor believers whom the Prophet taught Quran and religion morning and evening.
After the prohibition, the Prophet called the poor believers near, sat knee to knee with them, and waited until they rose; he thanked God for commanding him to live and die with them.
note: The companion command is also linked to 18:28.

view: The Prophet told destitute migrants listening to Quran that the poor would enter Paradise half a day, or five hundred years, before wealthy believers.
The Prophet said the gathering with poor believers resembled assemblies of earlier prophets and righteous people.
The Prophet warned Abu Bakr that upsetting Salman, Suhayb and Bilal would upset God; they then forgave Abu Bakr.
The poor Companions came early and sat near the Prophet to listen, prompting elites' objection to their precedence.
Some chiefs' pride made them refuse Islam after a low-status person had accepted first, lest they appear to follow him.
The Prophet refused actual expulsion, but considered or agreed to separate meeting times in hope of converting the leaders, without despising the poor.
note: Some report an initial agreement; these authors stress the aim of conversion.

view: Al-Hakim judged Sa'd's report by the criteria of al-Bukhari and Muslim, and Ibn Hibban also transmitted it.
Ibn Jarir also transmits the earlier account through Asbat.
The Prophet's contemplated separation of poor worshippers was not an actual expulsion, according to reports stressing the temporary arrangement.
The al-Aqra and Uyayna occasion is disputed: the verse is Meccan, while those men were associated with a later Medinan setting; it may be a later application of an earlier revelation.
Reports of discrete revelation occasions for this Meccan surah may describe applications, since it descended together; a reported Suffa occasion is rejected as anachronistic.
One account says the warning and no-expulsion verses descended together, while other reports leave their relation unspecified.
The verse forbids dismissing sincere poor worshippers to accommodate status-conscious elites and requires receiving, honoring, and remaining with them.
The verse applies broadly to anyone who believes in God and seeks His grace, even if their beliefs are incomplete; Quran followers should explain patiently rather than repel them.
The Prophet's concern for the wayward has limits: he should not neglect loyal seekers to court arrogant people.
Faith, reverence and conduct establish human worth; rank, wealth, lineage and fine clothing provide no ground to honor some while humiliating poor believers.
The leaders' demand echoes Noah's people disparaging his low-status followers; Noah likewise left their account to God and refused to expel them.
The instruction follows 6:51's warning to those who may become pious: the Prophet must stay with devout believers despite the leaders' arrogance.
The poor believers are linked with the preceding verse's people who believe in resurrection.
One parse makes the subjunctive verb answer the preceding negation of mutual accounting: their account cannot cause the Prophet to expel them.
An alternative makes 'then expel them' answer the prohibition itself, with the accounting clauses parenthetical; some object that it repeats 'do not expel, then expel.'
note: The repeated verb can reconnect the warning after the intervening clauses.

view: The account clauses can be parenthetical between the prohibition and its result regardless of whether their pronouns denote believers or polytheists.
A visit-without-conversation example is rejected as a model for this negation-result construction because it does not fit the verse's intended denial of expulsion and its cause.
Al-Alusi rejects attaching the result to the second denial if that would imply expulsion is proper whenever the Prophet bears the believers' account; he attaches it to the first denial.
An objection says coordination implies expulsion would be permissible if accountability existed; the reply says absence of responsibility is precisely why their expulsion would be unjust.
The invocation means performing obligatory prayer.
note: Some specify congregation.

view: Calling upon God means worship in general, including supplication, praise, obligatory and voluntary acts; no narrower reading is demonstrably required.
note: One argument cites Quranic use of 'call' for worship.

view: Calling upon God means remembering Him.
The believers recite or learn the Quran with the Prophet as their morning and evening devotion.
The phrase can mean literal supplication, asking God for refuge, guidance, or forgiveness with sincere monotheism.
Some understood the phrase as a remembrance or storytelling gathering after dawn prayer; Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and others objected that it referred to the congregational prayer just completed.
The protected people are marked by maintaining prayer in congregation.
The poor worshippers' invocation seeks God's pardon and forgiveness through duties, voluntary acts and remembrance.
The spiritual seeker's way is continual remembrance, sincere action and purity of the inner secret; elders should treat seekers gently and overlook slips.
Desiring God entails continual remembrance; a sincere seeker avoids unlike companions and seeks those of his own kind.
The servant directs every movement and stillness toward God, in response to his Lord.
A prophetic report says God is the companion of whoever remembers Him.
A Persian couplet likens worship without sincere intention to a grain without a kernel.
Al-ghadah denotes early morning, sometimes dawn prayer until sunrise; al-ashiyy denotes the late day, though one account extends it from noon toward dawn.
The morning form derives from ghudwah by changing its waw to alif, and al-ashiyy is derived from ashwa by changing waw to ya and assimilating.
These times are specified because people are busy then; devotion during busy hours implies even stronger devotion during free hours.
Morning stands for the day and evening for the night; sincere daytime worship implies still purer worship at night.
Most readers have bil-ghadah with alif and open ghayn; Ibn Amir and others read bil-ghudwah with waw and rounded ghayn, also in 18:28.
note: Sources vary in whether Ibn Amir is described as unique or one of several readers.

view: Ibn Abi Abla reads plural morning and evening forms, bil-ghadawat wal-ashiyyat; another reported reading has bil-ghadw without final ta.
Abu Ali favors the common ghadah: it is an indefinite noun that can take the article, whereas ghudwah is ordinarily a definite proper time name; spelling with waw alone proves no pronunciation.
note: The orthographic analogy is salah and zakah, written with waw but read with alif.

view: The ghudwah reading is supported by an indefinite dialect or a generic use of time names, allowing the article; al-Khalil compares duhwah, while some grammarians report tanwin.
note: Some defend genericizing a proper name; others cite an attested indefinite usage.

view: Abu Ubayd faulted the waw reading as following the script, while Abu Hayyan, al-Samin and al-Alusi defended oral transmission and the attested dialect.
note: The disagreement concerns whether spelling can establish recitation and whether ghudwah may take the article.

view: One analysis says ghudwah is an instance noun for a particular morning, while ghadah denotes morning generally, shifting the phrase from habitual to specific time.
At the time in question, prayer was performed as two units in the morning and two in the evening, before the five daily prayers were prescribed.
The two times identify the obligatory dawn and afternoon prayers.
note: Al-Alusi says these prayers are singled out for honor.

view: Morning and evening stand for all five daily obligatory prayers.
note: Ibrahim expressly rejects a storyteller-gathering interpretation.

view: One explanation identifies the evening prayer specifically as Isha.
Morning and evening denote continual, regular worship and remembrance rather than only those moments.
Morning and evening can stand metonymically for devotion performed at those times; prayer can likewise designate its time or place.
Al-ashiyy is likely synonymous with the singular ashiyyah, though a collective or plural analysis is reported; Quran 38:31 uses it of one evening.
The clause is circumstantial, attached to those who invoke; one analysis considers subject or object attachment but prefers the subject: they seek His face through invocation at those times.
Mentioning sincerity as their qualification highlights its centrality to worship and establishes their claim to honor.
Quraysh disparaged the poor believers as insincere followers seeking food, clothes or shelter rather than faith.
note: Ibn Ashur disputes a related accusation of hypocrisy.

view: Seeking God's face means sincerely seeking His favor or approval through worship and obedience, without worldly aims or ostentation.
note: Some phrase it as seeking reward; others stress no worldly benefit.

view: The worshippers seek God's reward, pardon, and nearness through righteous deeds, not partnership with Him.
Their public invocation professed faith in God alone and implies conviction; the claim that Quraysh accused them of hypocrisy lacks sound report.
For spiritual seekers, outward morning and evening acts coexist with uninterrupted inward desire and presence of heart before God.
The seeker exerts intention and effort, while the one sought receives divine enabling and rises through stations; both states are God's favor.
Spiritual desire is a heart's need that gives no rest until reaching God; poetic longing can carry the traveler fearlessly through wilderness.
The fully unified seek God's essence without reward, fear, attributes, intermediaries or awareness of themselves; their worship is heart-presence, spiritual witnessing and love.
God's testimony publicly confirms their inward sincerity; without it, no observer could confidently say a creature truly seeks God.
Their ragged appearance conceals ardent longing; God adorns chosen lovers with righteous acts and pure states although ordinary people do not see their rank.
They have no worldly or afterlife demand beyond their Master; devotion to Him draws His special care.
Face can denote the essence or reality of a thing as an honorific expression; thus seeking His face can mean seeking God Himself.
Another interpretation takes God's face as the direction, path, or obedience He commands people to pursue.
The beloved's face evokes love and longing to see God; seeking His face may thus signify seeking His approval or literally hoping for that vision.
note: Al-Alusi questions the metaphorical love account.

view: Anthropomorphists cite God's face as a bodily part; Razi and Abu Hayyan reject that, while Qurtubi also reports the description of God as possessing the Face.
note: The disagreement turns on whether 'face' denotes a bodily member.

view: Will ordinarily concerns originated possible things; describing seekers as willing God's eternal essence raises a theological difficulty requiring explanation.

God has no bodily face or material direction; face can name the aspect through which a thing is encountered, and divine names, attributes, religion, good deeds, and near-to-God beings are faces of God that endure by His permanence.
note: The grammatical argument at 55:27 is that 'possessor of majesty' describes the face.

words: مَا عَلَيْكَ مِنْ حِسَابِهِم مِّن شَىْءٍۢ
view: The first min can be partitive while the second is added for emphatic, comprehensive negation.

words: مَا عَلَيْكَ مِنْ حِسَابِهِم مِّن شَىْءٍۢ
view: In the first clause, ma may govern an accusative predicate or be inactive; alayka is a fronted predicate, min shay'in the subject, and min hisabihim may be a preceding circumstantial partitive rather than a delayed adjective.

words: مَا عَلَيْكَ مِنْ حِسَابِهِم مِّن شَىْءٍۢ
view: The genitive 'their accounting' may denote the Prophet accounting for the believers or the polytheists' reckoning of their poverty and weakness.

words: مَا عَلَيْكَ مِنْ حِسَابِهِم مِّن شَىْءٍۢ
view: Abu Hayyan calls al-Zamakhshari's paraphrase ungrammatical because 'his companion' lacks a singular antecedent; al-Samin suggests repairing it by supplying 'each one.'

words: مَا عَلَيْكَ مِنْ حِسَابِهِم مِّن شَىْءٍۢ وَمَا مِنْ حِسَابِكَ عَلَيْهِم مِّن شَىْءٍۢ
view: Both reciprocal clauses state the independence of each account; some say both are required, while others say the second reinforces the first though it could be omitted.
note: The disagreement concerns necessity versus emphasis of the repeated clause.

words: مَا عَلَيْكَ مِنْ حِسَابِهِم مِّن شَىْءٍۢ وَمَا مِنْ حِسَابِكَ عَلَيْهِم مِّن شَىْءٍۢ
view: Putting the Prophet first in both reciprocal clauses honors him; the reversal also forms a rhetorical return from ending to beginning.

words: مَا عَلَيْكَ مِنْ حِسَابِهِم مِّن شَىْءٍۢ
view: Fronting alayka conveys burden or obligation and may emphasize or restrict the negation; a restrictive reading confines the accounting to God.

words: مَا عَلَيْكَ مِنْ حِسَابِهِم مِّن شَىْءٍۢ وَمَا مِنْ حِسَابِكَ عَلَيْهِم مِّن شَىْءٍۢ
view: Two added min particles, fronting, reciprocal negation and possible restriction pile up emphasis against yielding to the chiefs' request.

words: مَا عَلَيْكَ مِنْ حِسَابِهِم مِّن شَىْءٍۢ
view: The reciprocal wording exposes the chiefs' pride disguised as advice: they pretended excluding the poor would win their belief and benefit the Prophet.

words: مَا عَلَيْكَ مِنْ حِسَابِهِم مِّن شَىْءٍۢ وَمَا مِنْ حِسَابِكَ عَلَيْهِم مِّن شَىْءٍۢ
view: Al-Alusi objects to al-Zamakhshari's treatment of the reciprocal denials as one thought like 'no bearer bears another's burden,' finding it an unfitting account of the wording.

words: مَا عَلَيْكَ مِنْ حِسَابِهِم مِّن شَىْءٍۢ وَمَا مِنْ حِسَابِكَ عَلَيْهِم مِّن شَىْءٍۢ
view: The Prophet and the poor worshippers each answer for their own deeds; God alone judges and assigns reward or punishment, so neither bears the other's account.
note: The no-bearer-bears-another's-burden principle is cited by several sources.

words: مَا عَلَيْكَ مِنْ حِسَابِهِم مِّن شَىْءٍۢ
view: The Prophet judges outward signs of piety; alleged hidden insincerity in the poor believers is their own account before God and cannot justify dismissing them.
note: Abu Hayyan objects that God already attests their sincerity.

words: مَا عَلَيْكَ مِنْ حِسَابِهِم مِّن شَىْءٍۢ
view: God's testimony of their sincerity makes a hypothetical blameworthy inner state inappropriate, according to Abu Hayyan.

words: مَا عَلَيْكَ مِنْ حِسَابِهِم مِّن شَىْءٍۢ وَمَا مِنْ حِسَابِكَ عَلَيْهِم مِّن شَىْءٍۢ
view: A competing explanation makes hisab provision or sufficiency: neither the Prophet nor the poor believers must maintain the other, because God provides for both.
note: Poverty therefore gives no reason to expel them.

words: مَا عَلَيْكَ مِنْ حِسَابِهِم مِّن شَىْءٍۢ
view: Ibn Ashur rejects making both parties' accounts God's alone as out of context and rendering the second clause redundant.
note: This conflicts with the widespread mutual-deeds interpretation.

words: مَا عَلَيْكَ مِنْ حِسَابِهِم مِّن شَىْءٍۢ
view: The poor are light in burden; God alone accounts for every person and gives the outcome of deeds.
Hisab originates in numerical counting and extends to measuring deeds for recompense; it can also mean sufficient provision, as illustrated by 78:36, 2:212 and Arabic usage of ahsabtuhu.
The accounting sentence may explain the prohibition or invalidate the chiefs' rationale for expulsion, with its separation marking a reason for the ban.
The pronouns in the reciprocal accounting clauses most apparently refer to the poor worshippers, as does the object of 'expel them.'
note: This is preferred against the polytheist-pronoun reading.

view: An alternative sends the account pronouns to the polytheists, while 'expel them' refers to the poor believers: the Prophet need not court the chiefs' conversion at his followers' expense.
note: The referent differs from the nearer poor-believer reading.

view: Ibn Ashur takes the clause as denying the Prophet responsibility for unbelievers' conversion, or their social reckoning of believers' poverty, so believers must retain their rights.
Al-Tabataba'i locates reward and therefore the reckoning of deeds with God alone.

words: وَمَا مِنْ حِسَابِكَ عَلَيْهِم مِّن شَىْءٍۢ
view: The parallel min hisabika is difficult to parse as a preceding circumstance because it would precede both its semantic governor and its possessor; an explanatory or predicate analysis is proposed.
One parse makes 'then you would be among wrongdoers' the subjunctive result of the initial prohibition, with the accounting and expulsion clauses intervening.
A competing parse coordinates 'be among wrongdoers' with 'expel them' as the consequence of the negation; wronging follows from expulsion.
Expelling innocent, sincere worshippers would wrong them by withholding the welcome and honor they deserve.
Another account says expulsion would wrong the Prophet himself through disobedience, loss or diminution of reward.
The conditional warning also depicts the chiefs' request itself as proud and unjust.
The Prophet would be wrong to disregard sincere believers for chiefs who might never believe; guidance belongs to God.
The warning is severe because the Prophet had considered giving wealthy leaders precedence over the weak.
The warning is conditional instruction and does not prove the Prophet actually expelled anyone, like the hypothetical warning against his associating partners with God.
Critics of prophetic impeccability say the episode shows the Prophet sinned by dismissing the poor; Razi replies he sought conversion, intended no contempt, and at most left a preferable course.
note: Razi also answers appeals to Noah's refusal and warnings against worldly adornment.

view: The wrongdoers are those who put a thing in the wrong place; the word can also express diminution.
